title: Tabuk
teaser: Thirty thousand men crossed the desert in high summer to fight an empire that never came out to meet them.

layers.title: The Setting
layers.subtitle: A knock at the door and the wrong question
layers.content:
The oil sellers brought the news. Nabateans who carried cooking oil from Ash-Sham down to Madinah reported that Heraclius was assembling an army in excess of forty thousand fighters, with the allied tribes of Lakhm and Judham among them, and that the advance force had already reached al-Balqa'.

The Byzantines had reason. An envoy of the Prophet ﷺ, al-Harith bin Umair al-Azdi, had been killed by Shurahbil bin Amr al-Ghassani while carrying a letter to the ruler of Busra, and the brigade sent to answer for it had fought the Byzantines at Mu'tah. Caesar could see the Arab tribes along his southern border beginning to calculate whether they still needed him. He decided the Muslim power had to be broken before it grew any larger.

In Madinah the fear was ordinary and visible. That year the Prophet ﷺ had taken an oath to stay away from his wives for a month, and the Companions could not work out why. Umar bin al-Khattab had an arrangement with a friend among the Ansar: whoever heard news first carried it to the other. One day the man hammered on his door. Open up, open up. Umar's first guess tells you what the city was thinking about. Have the Ghassanides come? No, said his friend, it is more serious than that. Allah's Messenger has deserted his wives.

Everything about the timing was wrong. It was the season of heat and drought, the harvest was near, and the road north was long and rough. Some in the city were glad of it: the hypocrites had built a mosque of their own, later called the Masjid of Harm, and asked him to come and pray in it and bless the place. He was on the point of leaving for Tabuk, so he put them off until his return.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari — Umar bin al-Khattab and his friend among the Ansar, 'have the Ghassanides come?'
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Army of Distress
layers.subtitle: Eighteen men to one animal, and leaves for food
layers.content:
He had always concealed his destination before a march. This time he named it. He told the people plainly that he intended to meet the Byzantines and fight them, and sent word to Makkah and the tribes to prepare. Part of Surat Bara'ah came down in those weeks, urging steadfastness, and he urged them to spend the best of their wealth.

They did. Uthman had two hundred saddled camels ready for a trading journey to Ash-Sham and gave all of them, with two hundred ounces of gold; then a hundred more camels and a thousand dinars. By the end his giving reached nine hundred camels and a hundred horses. Abdur-Rahman bin Awf gave two hundred ounces of silver. Umar gave half of what he owned. Abu Bakr gave everything he had and kept nothing for his family but Allah and His Messenger. Asim bin Adi sent ninety camel-loads of dates. One man brought half a kilo of dates, which was all he had. Women brought musk, armlets, anklets, earrings and rings. Only the hypocrites gave nothing, and they mocked the small gifts of the poor.

Some came asking for an animal to ride and there were none left. «تَوَلَّوا وَهُمْ تَفِيضُ أَعْيُنُهُمْ مِنَ الدَّمْعِ حَزَنًا» — they turned away with their eyes overflowing with tears of grief that they could find nothing to spend. (9:92)

Thirty thousand marched out on a Thursday in Rajab, the largest Muslim army yet assembled. It was also the worst equipped. Eighteen men took turns riding one mount. Men ate the leaves of trees until their lips swelled, and slaughtered camels they could not spare. The army was named for it: the Army of Distress.

He left Muhammad bin Maslamah over Madinah — another report names Siba' bin Urfutah — and gave Ali charge of his household. When the hypocrites used that against Ali and he rode after the column, he was sent back with: would it not suffice you to be my successor as Aaron was to Moses? Then he added that no prophet would succeed him.
layers.hadith_ref: Jami' at-Tirmidhi — 'nothing will harm Uthman after this day'; Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Military Expeditions
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Turning Point
layers.subtitle: They arrived, and nobody was there
layers.content:
The road did the fighting. Passing al-Hijr, where Thamud had cut their houses out of the rock, they drew water from its well and he forbade them to drink it or make wudu with it; dough already kneaded with it was to be fed to the camels. Do not enter the houses of those who wronged themselves, he said, lest what happened to them reach you — and if you must, let it be with weeping.

Water ran short and they complained. He asked, and a cloud came, and they drank. Near Tabuk he said that they would reach the spring the next day and no one was to touch its water before he came. Mu'adh bin Jabal reported what happened: two men had already reached it and admitted touching it; the spring gave only a thin trickle; the Prophet ﷺ scooped a little into his hands, washed his face and hands and poured it back, and water came out in quantity enough for the army. Mu'adh, he said, if you live long you will see this place under fields of vegetation.

Then the army camped at Tabuk and waited, and no enemy came. He gave a speech there, warning and encouraging men whose supplies were nearly gone. The Byzantines and their allies, hearing that thirty thousand had come out for them in that heat, did not advance. They scattered inside their own territory.

What followed was politics. Yuhannah bin Ru'bah, head of Aylah on the gulf, came in person, made peace and paid the jizyah, and received a written guarantee for his ships and caravans by land and sea. Jarba' and Adhruh did the same. Khalid bin al-Walid was sent with four hundred and fifty horsemen against Ukaydir, chief of Dumat al-Jandal, with a description of how he would find him: hunting wild cattle. He was taken outside his own castle gate on a moonlit night, spared, and made to pay in camels, cattle, armour and lances, and to collect tribute from Dumat, Tabuk, Aylah and Tayma'.

The tribes that had lived off Byzantine patronage understood that the arrangement was finished. The Muslim frontier now touched the empire's.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari — the well of al-Hijr and the houses of Thamud; Sahih Muslim — Mu'adh bin Jabal and the spring of Tabuk
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Revelation
layers.subtitle: The surah that read the city's mail
layers.content:
More of Surat at-Tawbah came down about this one expedition than about any battle he fought. Some verses before the march, some on the road, some after the return, and together they sorted the community by what it had actually done.

The march itself was given a name in the Book: «لَقَدْ تَابَ اللَّهُ عَلَى النَّبِيِّ وَالْمُهَاجِرِينَ وَالْأَنصَارِ الَّذِينَ اتَّبَعُوهُ فِي سَاعَةِ الْعُسْرَةِ» — 'Allah has certainly turned in mercy to the Prophet, and to the Emigrants and the Helpers who followed him in the hour of hardship.' (9:117) The men who had no mount and wept were excused by verse; so were the weak, the ill and those with nothing to spend, provided they were sincere to Allah and His Messenger (9:91). Those who sneered at the poor man's handful of dates were named too (9:79).

On the way home, on a mountain pass, twelve men tried to kill him. Only Ammar, holding the reins of his she-camel, and Hudhayfah bin al-Yaman, driving it, were with him; the rest of the army had gone down into the valley. They heard footsteps behind them, faces covered. Hudhayfah was sent back, struck the muzzles of their mounts with a crook, and they fled. He was told their names afterwards, which is why he is called the confidant. Of that night: «وَهَمُّوا بِمَا لَمْ يَنَالُوا» — 'and they resolved upon that which they could not attain.' (9:74)

Afterwards the leniency ended. He sent a party to demolish the mosque the hypocrites had built. The Muslims were forbidden to take their charity, to pray over their dead, to seek forgiveness for them or to visit their graves. Verses came down naming them openly, so that the whole city knew who they were.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: What It Left Behind
layers.subtitle: Fifty days of silence for three honest men
layers.content:
When Madinah came into view he said: this is a cheerful sight. This is Uhud, a mountain — we love it and it loves us. The town came out to meet the army, women and youths and small children, and The Sealed Nectar places here the singing of 'the white moon rose over us, through the valley of al-Wada'.'

He had gone in Rajab and come back in Ramadan. Fifty days in all, twenty of them at Tabuk. It was the last expedition he took part in personally.

He prayed two units in the mosque and then sat to receive people. More than eighty hypocrites came with excuses and oaths; he accepted the excuses and asked forgiveness for them, leaving what was inside them to Allah. Three men who had stayed behind for no reason at all did the opposite. Ka'b bin Malik, Murarah bin ar-Rabi' and Hilal bin Umayyah told the truth, and he directed the Companions not to speak to them. For over forty days nobody in the city addressed them. Then they were ordered away from their wives as well. Ka'b's own account is preserved at length in al-Bukhari: the earth, vast as it was, closed in on him.

On the fiftieth day the verse came: «وَعَلَى الثَّلَاثَةِ الَّذِينَ خُلِّفُوا حَتَّى إِذَا ضَاقَتْ عَلَيْهِمُ الْأَرْضُ وَضَاقَتْ عَلَيْهِمْ أَنفُسُهُمْ» — 'and to the three who were left behind, until the earth closed in upon them and their own selves closed in upon them... then He turned to them in mercy that they might repent.' (9:118) Ka'b called it the happiest day of his life.

Other things happened in that year. Negus of Abyssinia died and the Prophet ﷺ prayed the funeral prayer for him in absentia. His daughter Umm Kulthum died. Abdullah bin Ubayy, the head of the hypocrites, died after the return, and he prayed over him despite Umar's objection; a verse came later attesting to Umar's view.

Carry this. Eighty men lied and were let off in an afternoon. Three men told the truth and paid for fifty days, and it is their names the Qur'an keeps.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Military Expeditions — the long narration of Ka'b bin Malik on the expedition of Tabuk
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

quiz.prompt: How large was the Muslim army that marched to Tabuk?

options.text: Three thousand
Twelve thousand
Thirty thousand
Forty thousand

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the Muslim army leaves for Tabuk
quiz.scholar_reflection: Ten thousand marched on Makkah in 8 AH. Thirty thousand marched to Tabuk less than a year later. The size of that jump is one of the clearest measures of what the conquest changed.

quiz.prompt: Why is this campaign remembered as the Army of Distress?

options.text: The Muslims were defeated and withdrew
Eighteen men took turns on one mount, and men ate tree leaves until their lips swelled
A plague broke out in the camp at Tabuk
The Prophet ﷺ was ill for the whole journey

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the Muslim army leaves for Tabuk
quiz.scholar_reflection: It was the best funded expedition of his life and still short of everything. Uthman alone gave nine hundred camels and a hundred horses, and thirty thousand men still could not all ride.

quiz.prompt: What happened when the Muslim army reached Tabuk and camped?

options.text: A battle was fought that lasted three days
The Byzantines and their allies did not advance and scattered in their own territory
Heraclius came in person and accepted Islam
The army was ambushed at the spring

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the army of Islam at Tabuk
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Sealed Nectar judges that the political gains exceeded anything a battle could have produced. Aylah, Jarba', Adhruh and Dumat al-Jandal all came to terms without a fight.

quiz.prompt: Three believers stayed behind without an excuse and were boycotted until Allah forgave them. Who were they?

options.text: Ka'b bin Malik, Murarah bin ar-Rabi' and Hilal bin Umayyah
Abdullah bin Ubayy and two of his sons
Ammar, Hudhayfah and Mu'adh
Ka'b bin Zuhair, Zaid al-Khail and Adi bin Hatim

quiz.citation: Quran 9:118 and Sahih al-Bukhari — the narration of Ka'b bin Malik, cited in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: They were boycotted for over forty days, then separated from their wives, and forgiven on the fiftieth. The hypocrites who swore false oaths were forgiven the day the army got back.

quiz.prompt: Whom did the Prophet ﷺ send back to Madinah with the words 'would it not suffice you to be my successor as Aaron was to Moses?'

options.text: Muhammad bin Maslamah
Ali bin Abi Talib
Mu'adh bin Jabal
Siba' bin Urfutah

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the Muslim army leaves for Tabuk
quiz.scholar_reflection: Ali had been left in charge of the Prophet's household. The hypocrites used it to belittle him, so he rode after the army. He was sent back with that sentence, and with the addition that no prophet would succeed him.

quiz.prompt: Abu Bakr gave every single thing he owned. Umar gave half. Both are recorded with approval. Which of them would you rather be?

options.text: Abu Bakr — there is a kind of certainty that keeps nothing back
Umar — half is enormous and leaves a family provided for
It depends entirely on who else depends on you
Honestly, neither; I would have found a reason to give less

quiz.slider_label: Keep something back — Give the lot
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the Muslims race to donate for the expedition
quiz.scholar_reflection: The sirah records both without ranking them, and records beside them the man who brought half a kilo of dates because it was everything he had.

quiz.prompt: Men wept because there was no animal left for them to ride and nothing left for them to give. What does that reaction tell you?

options.text: They saw exclusion from the hardship as the loss, not the hardship itself
Poverty hurts most when it stops you doing something good
I am not sure I would weep; I might feel relief
Wanting to be counted in is not the same as wanting to go

quiz.slider_label: Relieved to be excused — Grieved to be excused
quiz.citation: Quran 9:92 — 'they turned away with their eyes overflowing with tears of grief that they could find nothing to spend'
quiz.scholar_reflection: The verse does not praise them for marching, because they did not march. It records the tears. Intention was accepted as the deed where the deed was impossible.

quiz.prompt: Eighty hypocrites lied about why they stayed home and were forgiven that afternoon. Three men admitted they had no excuse and were cut off from the whole city for fifty days. How does that sit with you?

options.text: The three were treated as believers, which is why anything was expected of them
It looks unjust until you see whose names the Qur'an kept
Honesty cost them fifty days and bought them a verse
I would probably have taken the excuse and the easy afternoon

quiz.slider_label: Offer the excuse — Tell the truth
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the people who lagged behind; Quran 9:118
quiz.scholar_reflection: Ka'b bin Malik said the earth closed in on him although it was vast — the same image the verse then used. He also called the day of his forgiveness the best day of his life.

quiz.prompt: Thirty thousand men crossed a desert in the worst season of the year and no battle took place. Was the expedition worth what it cost?

options.text: Yes — the border was settled and the client tribes changed sides
The cost was the point; it was a test that sorted the community
A threat answered early is cheaper than one answered at your own gates
It is fair to ask whether the Byzantine army was ever really coming

quiz.slider_label: Wait and see — Go and meet it
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the underlying reasons for the expedition of Tabuk
quiz.scholar_reflection: The reasoning given is that delay would have let the Byzantines reach Muslim provinces, or Madinah, while the hypocrites struck from inside. He chose to fight on their border rather than his own.

quiz.prompt: For the first time he announced his destination in advance instead of concealing it. Why do you think he dropped the secrecy here?

options.text: Nobody could be equipped for that march without knowing where it went
Announcing it forced everyone to declare themselves before it started
Surprise is worthless against an empire that already knows you exist
He wanted the Byzantines to hear, and they did

quiz.slider_label: Keep it hidden — Say it out loud
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — 'it was always the habit of the Prophet to conceal his intention... however this time he openly declared'
quiz.scholar_reflection: The declaration cost him nothing militarily and gained him a filter. By the time the column left Madinah, everyone in the city had already chosen a side in public.
